Global Chaos after Liberation Day Tariffs

By: Liz Fish | Commission

Proposal


Show:

Unique Selling Point:
The world economy and geopolitical order will never be the same, the last two weeks have seen chaos across global markets and trade relations after Trumps "Liberation Day" tariffs. Stock markets plummeted and are recovering with Musk adding 36 billion dollars to his fortune - was this all engineered by Trump and Musk? How do we make sense of this? We speak to Economist Dawie Roodt to give us the global economic perspective and impact locally. Roodt has weather many economic storms but says he has never lived through anything like this - even with the 90 day moratorium and 10% tariffs - the world will never be the same again. He as also never witnessed our own Budget go through this kind of turmoil and instability in the last 30 years. Stock markets once bitten twice shy, they will not invest as they have in the past. Roodt asks how long will the US dollar remain as the reserve currency? He predicts slower global economic growth, and inevitable growing unemployment in South Africa and the social instability and crime that goes with it.

What does all this mean for citrus farmer Gerrit Van Der Merwe in Citrusdal, who produce must hit the markets on time, or be lost to competitors. In the last two weeks they have been packing and picking oranges for export.

Summary:
SA is the 2nd largest exporter of citrus in the world, after Spain, and the largest in the Southern Hemisphere. It brings R33 Billion into our economy. Its labour intensive in an environment of 40% unemployment this is critical.
Busy picking right now, for the next few weeks fruit that would be destined for USA will go to Europe and the Middle East, but pretty quickly there will be an oversupply, markets flooded. Ecape and Limpopo export to those markets and so if WCApe diverts there they will be impacted.
In CT the shipping options are limited- Europe, middle East and the States - the Far East don’t even stop here because the port delays are so extreme
SA does not compete with USA Cirus farmers as we have the opposite/complementary seasons, and mandarins and oranges has been a growing market. Also USA is wealthiest markets, so its critical to keep our markets there
Gerrit has been exporting to USA for the last 25 years, they have an exporting importing company in Maine
Massive uncertainty currently – we need a clear policy decision- but with the GNU in its rocky state they extremely concerned
Biggest impact in rural areas - Already 40% unemployment- Cirtrusdal survived 2 floods, and two bad seasons, this year was a good season, fruit looking good and they hoped to begin to recover. Cirus is labour intensive and can create employment. They planted trees to expand the market which have just started bearing and by 2030 they were going to generate 100 000 jobs.


Further information:
Farmers will have to start cutting costs, social development impacted. ALG spends 1 million on social development annually. 50 University scholarships. Private schooling for 150 kids and that in one farm

Extra Budget Items:
Travel to Citrusdal and overnight accommodation.

Dawie Roodt
Gerrit Van Der Merwe

Script:


Gerrit: “We farm for The USA, and that's actually where our money comes from.
Trump” One bill is going to straighten out our country for many many years to come “
Gerrit: Nobody really knows what comes next week because we're in a very, very shape shifting world economy.
Dawie: We're seeing somebody doing really wacko things like increasing tariffs by sillier percentages, based on completely incorrect calculations
Trump: “ And we said just let do it, let's just get it done”
Dawie: This is like somebody playing in a in a lab.

VO: Two men - on opposite sides of the country - doing very different jobs.
PAUSE
VO: But what they have in common is a shared fear about what a seismic shift in America’s international trade policy - means for our country - and their futures. One an economist, attempting to predict the future - the other - a citrus farmer trying to survive the present.
FTB
VO: Gerrit Van Der Merwe’s family have been farming in Citrusdal, in the Western Cape, for 8 generations. Surviving droughts, floods, and sanctions, they’ve spent the last 25 years - building a market - in the USA.
TRUMP” The markets are going to boom, and the rest of the world wants to see if there is any way they can make a deal,
VO: It’s a market now under threat following an announcement by American President, Donald Trump, that most South African goods will no longer be imported into his country - tariff free.
Breather
ERIN “Do you remember your reaction on hearing the actual 31% for South Africa?
Gerrit: Yeah, I was actually off that day, and I was awake at half past four in the morning looking at the news, and then my holiday was done.
Breather- Up sound “Hoeweel het jou op die oomblik …gestamp
VO: Trump has made no secret of his belief that America is being taken advantage of; a victim he believes of a system of global trade - unfairly targeting American exports for tariffs.
On the 2nd of April - he announced a sweeping new tariff regime - including a 31% duty on our exports. Trump called it Liberation Day.
Upsound Trump applause

Link: “The relationship between suited economists and analysts and farmers toiling in the blazing sun might not be immediately obvious. But their livelihoods and lives collide. The former build reputations making predictions about the short and long term future”
“ and the farmers rely on those predictions when making important business decisions…

ERIN: “How are you coping?
Gerrit: “ As a farmer, you're very emotionally involved in what you do. I mean, every single orange that goes out this out the packing has almost got a name. ….But, unfortunately, that passion leads to anxiety. So not knowing where to go and how to go is probably one of our biggest challenges now
Trump Upsound” I did a 90 day pause for those people who didn't retaliate”
VO: After his Liberation Day announcement, Trump announced a 90 day pause on the new tariffs, replacing them with a 10% duty, while excluding critical minerals.
It didn’t do much to relieve global anxiety.
Upsound Trump “ I just want fair deals for everybody”
Dawie: “ We should be scared. Globally, there is there are a lot of things happening. The world is changing.
VO: Dawie Roodt’s working day starts at 3am. First on his list are the exchange rates between the various major currencies, after that he looks at the equity markets and then the news - that means he was awake when Trump made his startling tariff announcement.
Dawie: “Looking at this and knowing that today, a couple of billion rand is going to be wiped off to the JSE, I can see that coming before it happened, before the markets open we see this in real time
VO: Dawie says, in the 40 years he’s been an economist, he’s never known anything as turbulent or confusing as the past few weeks.
Dawie: “Tariffs what it does it disrupts international trade because all of a sudden it's got an impact on prices. making it more expensive for American consumers to buy these things, having an impact on the capital market, and the result of all of this was well mayhem.
” So this is scary. It's scary to see what's gonna happen, what the impact is gonna be on all sort of things in the economy, because what we are seeing here are experiments.
Masa: Do we understand why it's being done?
Dawie “So what's been happening is the Americans consume more than what they produce for a very long time and that's what Donald Trump doesn't like. He says that's wrong.
TRUMP UPSOUND Journalist: “ How is it going?
Trump “ I think its going very well we have 6 or 7 trillion dollars coming into our country and we have never seen anything like it “
VO: But that means there is a lot at stake for the South African citrus industry, they expected to export more than 7 million cartons of fruit to the US, employing 35 000 people, generating 2 billion rand in foreign revenue. A punishing tariff regime – 90 days breather or not – would be potentially devastating to this community.
VO: It’s an environment in which, for now, doing nothing - is doing something.
Gerrit “We just came out of the two day board meeting, and what we decided, we're not gonna decide anything , that after a two day session, so ja, there is a lot of uncertainty
Link : Donald Trump is an avid golfer as appears to spend as much time on the tee-box - as he does in the Oval Office. And that didn’t change, even as the world was reeling from his so-called Liberation Day tariffs.
It’s still not clear what Trumps ultimate goal is and whether his recent backtracking is part of a broader strategy - or - he miscalculated the fallout.
LINK : Whatever the reason, it’s left us all wondering what other surprises lie in store … and what damage they might do.
VO: As the anxiety deepens, Gerrit is trying to be philosophical, when it comes to motivating his staff.
Upsound “Ok ons kan daai ding raak kry
Gerrit: You can't give them all the news , You're trying to give them enough information for them to go forward. But there's no point in fear mongering your management.
ERIN VO: Ironically, he relies on a comparison Trump probably wouldn’t understand.
Gerrit “I think it's like a half time rugby speech when you're 14 points behind, and you're trying to catch up, and you have to keep the guys positive .
Upsound Gerrit “This is a very late area because its close to the river
VO: The truth is that markets hate uncertainty… and so does fruit. Trump may feel like his offered countries like South Africa a reprieve - but that’s not how Gerrit sees it.
Gerrit “Yes we have 90 days but it takes about 30 days shipping to the USA so we actually only have 60 days before we have to make a call so it puts us really at a disadvantage because we can't ship the product towards the end of June and then it gets there with 30 % tariff “
LINK : Citrusdal has been through a lot over the past few years, not least two devastating floods. But recently, things were looking up: this year’s crop was good and farmers here were looking forward - to a bumper export
Masa: But Donald Trump had other plans: and even though he’s given the world a 90-day breather, how does anyone supposed plan in this environment?”
Dawie “ Don't do anything irrational right now, don’t run out there and try to sell everything. Sit on your hands and wait this out
Erin “ Gerrit it looks like there have also been some new trees planted
Gerrit “For the South African industry we have a goal by 2032 to create 100 000 jobs of all the new hectares coming in so hopefully it can be a solution for the SA economy
VO: Here sitting on your hands isn’t a long-term option. It takes years for trees to mature, and business plans - are made decades in advance.
ERIN “And I guess you grew those thinking about the US market?
Gerrit “ US is one of our prime markets all our planning and all our cultivars we have planted is to fill gaps we see is needed in the US market, now that is not necessarily the same thing as going to Euroupe or India or to Far East
ERIN “Shew, so the change in tariffs could really throw a spanner into the works for your forward planning for the next couple of years?
Gerrit “ Yes you would probably have to reshape your cultivar structure and when do you plant and when do you harvest it
Breather
LINK : Gerrit’s Citrus export business began the same year the African Growth and Opportunity Act was passed in 2000
Now that’s the famous AGOA that everyone keeps talking about. It means farmers like Gerrit have been able to send his citrus to the US - without paying for duties.
But, Trump’s tariffs override AGOA, effectively bring duty-free trade to a stop, and leaving Gerrit and others wondering: now what?
VO: The short-term answer to that, is for our government to move on a trade agreement with the US, that’s beneficial to both countries. With just 90 days to do it - the pressure’s on.
Gerrit “ If you can if you can get this deal done and over the line and save 35,000 jobs in the Western Northern Cape, that's a win. And I think the government at the moment, politics needs a win in South Africa.
ERIN: “Do you have confidence they can?
Gerrit “Yes, we are very confident, but yet very anxious.
Masa “What should the South African government be doing right now in terms of engaging with the US government? Also considering that there are tensions between the two governments.?
Dawie: We are a minnow. We are a tiny, tiny economy. We have to understand that we do not have the economic muscle. We've got an unstable basically unstable political situation in South Africa. We are dealing with the strongest man in the world. He could be a bully, but he is the biggest bully on the playground and he's got an ego. So the best you can do go sit in the corner and be very very quiet.
VO: So what advice does Dawie have for these farmers?
Dawie” In the case of farmers, try to find other markets and there are big markets out there. The Indian market is a big market that is gradually opening up, we are already doing a lot of business with the Chinese
VO: But that's easier said than done. It took twenty years to build the South African citrus market in the US, and Gerrit’s business alone - employs 20 000 Americans.
Gerrit “What we've done in The US market, we've become extremely competitive. The whole industry is very intertwined. You need a cold room. You need a trucker. You need a forklift driver. You need confidence and supply on that side. If you don't have that, that's not built in a year. That's built in five to seven to eight years.
LINK So where do we go from here- and where do these go
The Trump administration is so unpredictable that all we can be certain about right now is nothing is certain and the entire world is in for a rocky ride.

metadata.Unique Selling Point: The world economy and geopolitical order will never be the same, the last two weeks have seen chaos across global markets and trade relations after Trumps "Liberation Day" tariffs. We speak to Economist Dawie Roodt to give us the global economic perspective and impact locally. Roodt has weather many economic storms but says he has never lived through anything like this - even with the 90 day moratorium and 10% tariffs - the world will never be the same again. He as also never witnessed our own Budget go through this kind of turmoil and instability in the last 30 years. Stock markets once bitten twice shy, they will not invest as they have in the past. Roodt asks how long will the US dollar remain as the reserve currency? He predicts slower global economic growth, and inevitable growing unemployment in South Africa and the social instability and crime that goes with it.
